_meta.notes: Comprehensive index for France covering Gaul (Vercingetorix, Caesar's conquest 52 BCE), Frankish kingdoms (Clovis I 481, Merovingians, Carolingians), Charlemagne (Holy Roman Emperor 800), Capetian dynasty, Hundred Years' War (1337-1453, Joan of Arc), Renaissance, Wars of Religion (St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre 1572), Louis XIV Sun King (Versailles, absolute monarchy), French Revolution 1789 (storming Bastille, Declaration of Rights, Terror, Robespierre), Napoleon Bonaparte (Emperor 1804-15, Napoleonic Wars, Code Napoleon), Restoration/July Revolution 1830/1848 Revolution, Second Empire (Napoleon III), Franco-Prussian War 1870, Third Republic, Dreyfus Affair, WWI (Verdun, 1.4M dead), WWII (Fall of France 1940, Vichy regime, Free France/de Gaulle, D-Day liberation), Fourth Republic, Algerian War (1954-62), Fifth Republic (de Gaulle), May 1968, EU founding member, and cultural superpower.

religion.note: Laïcité (strict secularism since 1905 separation law); 'Eldest Daughter of the Church' historically; Catholic declining rapidly; Muslim largest in Europe (~5.7M); Jewish (~450k, largest in Europe, Dreyfus Affair legacy); headscarf/burkini debates; religion deeply private; anti-clericalism strong tradition

ethnic_groups.name: French (no official ethnic statistics)
ethnic_groups.notes: France does not collect ethnic/racial data (republican universalism: 'all citizens are French'); estimated ethnic French ~75-80%; strong assimilationist model; regional identities (Breton, Alsatian, Corsican, Basque, Occitan)

ethnic_groups.name: North African/Maghrebi origin
ethnic_groups.notes: Estimated ~5-6M+ (Algerian, Moroccan, Tunisian); colonial legacy; banlieue concentrations; integration challenges; 2005 riots; discrimination

ethnic_groups.name: Sub-Saharan African origin
ethnic_groups.notes: Estimated ~4-5M (West/Central Africa, Caribbean DOM-TOM); colonial legacy; francophone immigration; cultural contributions

ethnic_groups.name: European immigrant origin
ethnic_groups.notes: Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, Polish (waves 19th-20th century); fully assimilated; 'invisible immigrants'

ethnic_groups.name: Overseas territories
ethnic_groups.notes: Guadeloupe, Martinique, Réunion, French Guiana, Mayotte, New Caledonia, Polynesia; diverse (Afro-Caribbean, Creole, Melanesian, Polynesian); French citizens

country_profile.time_zone: CET (UTC+1) / CEST (UTC+2); plus 12 time zones (overseas territories)

independence.from: Treaty of Verdun (West Francia); Revolution 1789 (modern republic)

country_profile.notes_unique: French Revolution 1789 (transformed world: 'Liberté, Égalité, Fraternité', Declaration of Rights of Man, abolished feudalism, executed Louis XVI); Napoleon (conquered Europe, Code Civil/Napoleon still basis of law in 70+ countries); colonial empire (second largest ever, Africa/Asia/Americas); Paris ('City of Light', Eiffel Tower, Louvre, Notre-Dame); nuclear power (70%+ electricity, independent nuclear deterrent); UN P5 member; EU founding member (Schuman Declaration 1950, with Germany); cultural superpower (cuisine UNESCO, fashion, wine, cheese, philosophy, literature: Hugo/Proust/Camus/Sartre; cinema: Lumière Brothers, New Wave; Impressionism: Monet/Renoir); laïcité (secularism); 49 UNESCO World Heritage Sites (4th most); Tour de France; most visited country in world (~90M tourists/year); D-Day (June 6, 1944, Normandy); Algerian War (1954-62, 1.5M+ dead, trauma); Yellow Vests 2018-19; pension protests 2023

current_leader.name: Emmanuel Macron
current_leader.title: President
current_leader.notes: La République En Marche/Renaissance; youngest president since Napoleon III (39); centrist; ex-investment banker (Rothschild); married to former teacher (25 years older); defeated Le Pen twice (2017, 2022); pension reform (pushed through without parliament vote, Article 49.3); dissolved parliament 2024 (backfired, hung parliament); EU integration champion; 'Jupiter' presidency; Ukraine support

prime_minister.name: François Bayrou
prime_minister.title: Prime Minister
prime_minister.notes: MoDem; centrist veteran; fourth PM in 2024 (political instability); minority government; budget crisis

former_leaders.name: François Hollande
former_leaders.notes: PS (Socialist); defeated Sarkozy; deeply unpopular (lowest polls in 5th Republic history); terrorism crises (Charlie Hebdo January 2015, Bataclan November 2015, Nice July 2016); same-sex marriage 2013; did not seek re-election

former_leaders.name: Nicolas Sarkozy
former_leaders.notes: UMP/LR; 'hyper-president'; Hungarian-Jewish origin; Libya intervention 2011 (Gaddafi overthrown); financial crisis; convicted corruption (3 years, 1 suspended); multiple trials; polarising

former_leaders.name: Jacques Chirac
former_leaders.notes: RPR/UMP; two terms; opposed Iraq War 2003 (US-France rift, 'freedom fries'); acknowledged Vichy complicity in Holocaust (1995 speech, historic); nuclear tests controversy; died 2019

former_leaders.name: François Mitterrand
former_leaders.notes: PS; first Socialist president of 5th Republic; two terms (14 years, longest); abolished death penalty 1981; Grands Projets (Louvre Pyramid, BnF); Maastricht Treaty; European integration; Vichy past revealed; died 1996

former_leaders.name: Charles de Gaulle
former_leaders.notes: Founder of Fifth Republic; Free France leader (WWII resistance from London, 'La France libre'); liberated Paris 1944; Algerian independence (controversial); nuclear weapons program; NATO withdrawal (1966); 'Vive le Québec libre!'; May 1968 crisis; resigned 1969; greatest Frenchman (polls); de Gaulle airport; towering 20th-century figure

910.name: Prehistoric Gaul
910.description: France possesses some of Europe's most spectacular prehistoric sites, from the Palaeolithic cave paintings at Lascaux and Chauvet to megalithic monuments in Brittany, representing tens of thousands of years of human creativity.

sub_clusters.name: Lascaux & Palaeolithic Cave Art
sub_clusters.description: The Lascaux cave paintings (c. 17,000 BCE), Chauvet cave (c. 32,000 BCE), and the rich Upper Palaeolithic cultures of the Dordogne and Pyrenees regions.
key_events: Creation of the Lascaux cave paintings (c. 17,000 BCE)
Chauvet cave art – among the oldest known figurative paintings (c. 32,000 BCE)

sub_clusters.name: Neolithic & Megalithic France
sub_clusters.description: The Carnac stone alignments in Brittany, dolmens, the spread of agriculture, and proto-Celtic cultures preceding the La Tène period.

910.name: Celtic Gaul & Roman Conquest
910.description: Celtic Gaul was a culturally vibrant mosaic of tribes until Caesar's conquest (58–50 BCE) transformed it into one of Rome's wealthiest provinces, producing cities like Lugdunum (Lyon) and Narbo (Narbonne).

sub_clusters.name: Celtic Gaul & La Tène Culture
sub_clusters.description: The diverse Gallic tribes (Arverni, Aedui, Sequani), Greek colonisation at Massalia (Marseille), oppida settlements, and the Gallic warrior culture.

sub_clusters.name: Caesar's Gallic Wars
sub_clusters.description: Julius Caesar's eight-year campaign to conquer Gaul, Vercingetorix's resistance and defeat at Alesia (52 BCE), and the transformation of Gaul into a Roman province.
key_events: Siege of Alesia – Vercingetorix surrenders to Caesar (52 BCE)

sub_clusters.name: Roman Gaul & Gallo-Roman Civilisation
sub_clusters.description: The flourishing of Gallo-Roman culture, construction of amphitheatres (Nîmes, Arles), aqueducts (Pont du Gard), Christianisation, and the eventual Frankish settlement.

920.name: Frankish Kingdom & Carolingian Empire
920.description: Clovis's conversion to Christianity and unification of the Franks created the foundations of France. Charlemagne's empire represented the apex of early medieval power, and its division at Verdun (843) defined France's eastern borders for centuries.

sub_clusters.name: Clovis & the Merovingian Dynasty
sub_clusters.description: Clovis I's baptism, unification of the Frankish tribes, the Merovingian 'do-nothing kings', and the rise of Carolingian mayors of the palace.
key_events: Clovis I baptised as a Catholic Christian (c. 496 CE)

sub_clusters.name: Charlemagne & the Carolingian Empire
sub_clusters.description: Charlemagne's imperial coronation (800 CE), the Carolingian Renaissance, and the Treaty of Verdun (843) dividing the empire into West Francia, East Francia, and Lotharingia.
key_events: Charlemagne crowned Emperor by Pope Leo III (800 CE)
Treaty of Verdun divides the Carolingian Empire (843)

sub_clusters.name: Late Carolingian & Capetian Transition
sub_clusters.description: Viking raids on Paris (845, 885–886), the weakening of Carolingian authority, and the election of Hugh Capet in 987 founding the dynasty that would rule France for over 800 years.

920.name: Capetian Dynasty & Medieval France
920.description: The Capetian kings gradually built France into Europe's most powerful kingdom through administrative centralisation, Gothic cathedral construction, crusading prestige, and the suppression of the Cathars and Templars.

sub_clusters.name: Early Capetians & the Crusades
sub_clusters.description: Hugh Capet's election, the First Crusade's French leadership (Godfrey of Bouillon), the Albigensian Crusade against Cathar heresy, and Philip II Augustus's expansion of royal power.

sub_clusters.name: Louis IX & High Medieval France
sub_clusters.description: Saint Louis's ideal of Christian kingship, the building of Sainte-Chapelle, Philip IV's conflict with Pope Boniface VIII, the suppression of the Knights Templar (1307), and the Avignon Papacy.

930.name: Hundred Years' War & Joan of Arc
930.description: The epic Anglo-French conflict that devastated France for over a century, featuring the disasters of Crécy and Agincourt, the Burgundian civil war, and Joan of Arc's miraculous intervention that turned the tide.

sub_clusters.name: Early Hundred Years' War
sub_clusters.description: Edward III's claim to the French throne, the catastrophic French defeats at Crécy (1346) and Poitiers (1356), the Black Death, the Jacquerie peasant revolt, and the Treaty of Brétigny.

sub_clusters.name: Agincourt & Burgundian Crisis
sub_clusters.description: The madness of Charles VI, the Armagnac-Burgundian civil war, Henry V's victory at Agincourt (1415), the Treaty of Troyes disinheriting the Dauphin, and the nadir of French fortunes.
key_events: Battle of Agincourt – Henry V defeats French forces (1415)

sub_clusters.name: Joan of Arc & French Recovery
sub_clusters.description: Joan of Arc's relief of Orléans (1429), Charles VII's coronation at Reims, Joan's capture and execution (1431), and the final French reconquest ending English presence on the continent.
key_events: Joan of Arc lifts the Siege of Orléans (1429)
Joan of Arc burned at the stake in Rouen (1431)

930.name: Wars of Religion & Early Modern France
930.description: France's Italian Wars ambitions gave way to devastating civil wars between Catholics and Huguenots, marked by the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre and resolved only by Henry IV's Edict of Nantes.

sub_clusters.name: Italian Wars & Renaissance France
sub_clusters.description: French invasions of Italy, Francis I's patronage of Leonardo da Vinci, the châteaux of the Loire Valley, and the Peace of Cateau-Cambrésis ending Franco-Habsburg rivalry in Italy.

sub_clusters.name: French Wars of Religion
sub_clusters.description: Eight civil wars between Catholics and Huguenots, the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre (1572), the War of the Three Henrys, and Henry IV's conversion and Edict of Nantes (1598).
key_events: St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre (24 August 1572)
Edict of Nantes grants Huguenot religious rights (1598)

930.name: Absolutism & Louis XIV
930.description: The construction of absolute monarchy under Richelieu, Mazarin, and Louis XIV—the Sun King—who built Versailles, revoked the Edict of Nantes, and made France the dominant power in Europe.

sub_clusters.name: Richelieu, Mazarin & the Fronde
sub_clusters.description: Cardinal Richelieu's centralisation of power, French intervention in the Thirty Years' War, Cardinal Mazarin's regency, the Fronde rebellions, and the foundations of absolute monarchy.

sub_clusters.name: The Sun King & Versailles
sub_clusters.description: Louis XIV's personal rule, the construction of Versailles, the revocation of the Edict of Nantes (1685), the War of the Spanish Succession, and France as the cultural model of Europe.
key_events: Construction of the Palace of Versailles (1661–1715)
Revocation of the Edict of Nantes (1685)

940.name: The French Revolution
940.description: The French Revolution transformed not only France but the entire Western world, overthrowing the ancien régime, proclaiming the Rights of Man, and unleashing both democratic ideals and revolutionary terror.

sub_clusters.name: Fall of the Bastille & Constitutional Monarchy
sub_clusters.description: The Estates-General crisis, the storming of the Bastille (14 July 1789), the Declaration of the Rights of Man, the Women's March on Versailles, the Civil Constitution of the Clergy, and the constitutional monarchy experiment.
key_events: Storming of the Bastille (14 July 1789)
Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (August 1789)

sub_clusters.name: Republic, Terror & Thermidor
sub_clusters.description: The execution of Louis XVI (1793), the Reign of Terror under Robespierre, the Committee of Public Safety, the Thermidorian Reaction, and the Directory's unstable governance.
key_events: Execution of Louis XVI (21 January 1793)
Fall of Robespierre and end of the Terror (27 July 1794)

940.name: The Napoleonic Era
940.description: Napoleon Bonaparte's rise from Corsican artillery officer to Emperor of France, his revolutionary legal and administrative reforms, his conquest of most of Europe, and his ultimate defeat at Waterloo.

sub_clusters.name: Consulate & Empire
sub_clusters.description: The coup of 18 Brumaire, the Napoleonic Code, the Concordat with the Pope, the imperial coronation (1804), Austerlitz, Jena, and the Continental System against Britain.
key_events: Napoleon crowns himself Emperor (2 December 1804)
Promulgation of the Napoleonic Code (1804)

sub_clusters.name: Fall of Napoleon
sub_clusters.description: The catastrophic Russian campaign (1812), the Battle of Leipzig, Napoleon's first abdication and exile to Elba, the Hundred Days, and the final defeat at Waterloo (18 June 1815).

940.name: Nineteenth-Century France
940.description: A turbulent century of political upheaval—Restoration, July Monarchy, Second Republic, Second Empire, and Third Republic—alongside colonial expansion, the Dreyfus Affair, and the Franco-Prussian War's humiliation.

sub_clusters.name: Restoration & Revolutions (1830, 1848)
sub_clusters.description: The Bourbon Restoration, the July Revolution (1830) installing Louis-Philippe, the February Revolution (1848) creating the Second Republic, and Louis-Napoleon's coup establishing the Second Empire.

sub_clusters.name: Second Empire & Colonial Expansion
sub_clusters.description: Napoleon III's modernisation of Paris (Haussmann), the Second Empire's economic boom, colonial conquests in Algeria, Indochina, and West Africa, and the disastrous Franco-Prussian War.

sub_clusters.name: Franco-Prussian War & Third Republic
sub_clusters.description: The humiliating defeat of 1870, the Paris Commune (1871), the establishment of the Third Republic, the Dreyfus Affair, laïcité (1905), and the building of the colonial empire.
key_events: Franco-Prussian War and loss of Alsace-Lorraine (1870–1871)
Dreyfus Affair polarises French society (1894–1906)

950.name: France in World War I
950.description: France bore the heaviest burden of the Western Front, with the Battle of Verdun becoming a symbol of national determination. The war cost 1.4 million French dead and devastated northern France.

sub_clusters.name: Battle of Verdun & the Western Front
sub_clusters.description: The Miracle of the Marne (1914), the inferno of Verdun (1916), the Nivelle Offensive mutinies (1917), and the final Allied victory with France's territorial recovery of Alsace-Lorraine.
key_events: Battle of Verdun – 'Ils ne passeront pas' (1916)
French army mutinies after Nivelle Offensive (1917)

950.name: France in World War II
950.description: The stunning Fall of France (1940), the Vichy regime's collaboration, de Gaulle's Free France movement, the Resistance, and the liberation of Paris represented the darkest and most heroic chapters of French history.

sub_clusters.name: Fall of France & Vichy Regime
sub_clusters.description: The German blitzkrieg, the armistice, Marshal Pétain's Vichy regime, collaboration in the Holocaust (Vel d'Hiv roundup), and the division between occupied and 'free' zones.

sub_clusters.name: Free France, Resistance & Liberation
sub_clusters.description: De Gaulle's 18 June appeal, the Free French Forces, the growing internal Resistance (Jean Moulin), D-Day and the liberation of Paris (August 1944), and the épuration (purge).
key_events: De Gaulle's Appeal of 18 June from London (1940)
Liberation of Paris (25 August 1944)

950.name: Decolonisation & Fourth Republic
950.description: The Fourth Republic struggled with colonial wars in Indochina and Algeria that consumed French politics, culminating in the Algerian crisis that brought de Gaulle back to power and created the Fifth Republic.

sub_clusters.name: Indochina War
sub_clusters.description: The First Indochina War against the Viet Minh, the catastrophic defeat at Dien Bien Phu (1954), and the Geneva Accords ending French rule in Southeast Asia.

sub_clusters.name: Algerian War & Birth of the Fifth Republic
sub_clusters.description: The Algerian War of Independence, the FLN insurgency, the use of torture, the May 1958 crisis, de Gaulle's return and creation of the Fifth Republic, and the Évian Accords granting Algerian independence.
key_events: Battle of Algiers (1957)
De Gaulle founds the Fifth Republic (1958)

960.name: Fifth Republic & Gaullism
960.description: De Gaulle's Fifth Republic established a strong presidential system, pursued French nuclear independence (force de frappe), withdrew from NATO's military command, and navigated the revolutionary upheaval of May 1968.

sub_clusters.name: De Gaulle Presidency
sub_clusters.description: De Gaulle's strong presidency, the force de frappe nuclear programme, withdrawal from NATO military command, vetoing British EEC entry, and the crisis of May 1968.
key_events: May 1968 – student and worker uprising shakes France

sub_clusters.name: Post-Gaullist Transition
sub_clusters.description: The presidencies of Pompidou and Giscard d'Estaing, economic modernisation, the lowering of the voting age, and the preparation for the Mitterrand era.

960.name: Contemporary France
960.description: France's evolution under the Fifth Republic through Mitterrand's socialist experiment, Chirac's cohabitation, the EU's founding partnership with Germany, and contemporary challenges of terrorism, immigration, and populism.

sub_clusters.name: Mitterrand Era & EU Integration
sub_clusters.description: Mitterrand's presidency, the socialist reforms, the Maastricht Treaty and deeper EU integration, the Franco-German engine of Europe, and the grands projets (Louvre Pyramid, Bastille Opera).

sub_clusters.name: Chirac, Sarkozy & Republican Challenges
sub_clusters.description: The 2005 banlieue riots, the rejection of the EU constitution, Sarkozy's presidency, debates over laïcité and Muslim integration, and France's role in NATO's return.

sub_clusters.name: Terrorism, Yellow Vests & Modern France
sub_clusters.description: The Hollande and Macron presidencies, the Charlie Hebdo and Bataclan terrorist attacks (2015), the Yellow Vests movement (2018), pension reform protests, and France's EU leadership role.
key_events: Charlie Hebdo and November 2015 Paris terrorist attacks
Yellow Vests (Gilets Jaunes) movement erupts (2018)

unassigned_events.note: Events not yet assigned to a thematic cluster
